articles.title: Why AI Is Vacuuming Up the World’s Wealth
articles.summary: A lot of cash flying around the globe is going to one place. That’s a potential problem for the US, developing nations and maybe the global economy.
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- There's more money flying around the world than ever, and a lot of it is headed to one place: artificial intelligence. That could become a problem for the US government, developing nations and the global economy.

In this weekly documentary by Bloomberg Originals, we unpack how the AI boom has quickly concentrated wealth not only in those seven companies Wall Street calls magnificent, but the firms and nations profiting from the technology's massive buildout. One problem? Money that would otherwise be buying sovereign debt or investing in developing nations and traditional industries is instead being funneled into a riskier bet with no guarantee of return. Meanwhile, the massive shift in capital is pushing global trade imbalances to levels unseen since 2008. And we all know what happened then.

Companies in South Korea, Japan and Taiwan are the main producers of semiconductors critical to the data centers sprouting up all over the US. That's led to vast amounts of cash piling up — courtesy of the US tech giants buying those chips — and a search for good return. In some cases, that cash is heading right back into stocks and bonds issued by those same American AI companies.

Historical analyses show that the more flush those economies become, the greater the risk tolerance when it comes to where all that cash is invested. And that reality is playing out right now, as more money pours into equities and corporate bonds rather than lower-risk investments like US Treasuries. Witness the rising yields of US government debt, as well as that of other nations, and you begin to see just how big an impact the AI revolution is having — and the grave consequences if it falls short.

articles.title: Inteligência Artificial sai da tela e ganha forma humana no Siará Tech Summit  | G1
articles.standfirst: Robô humanoide que circula pelo evento mostra, na prática, novas possibilidades de integração entre inteligência artificial, robótica e interação com o público
articles.summary: Robô humanoide que circula pelo evento mostra, na prática, novas possibilidades de integração entre inteligência artificial, robótica e interação com o público
articles.body:
Fred, o robô humanoide — Foto: Sebrae/CE

Entre palestras, startups e espaços de networking, um personagem diferente tem chamado a atenção de quem circula pelo Siará Tech Summit. Sucesso no primeiro dia do evento, nesta quarta-feira (7), O Fred Interage, robô humanoide que participa do evento, conversa com visitantes, posa para fotos e interage com o público, transformando em experiência prática uma tecnologia que ainda costuma estar associada às telas de computadores e celulares.

O projeto é desenvolvido pela Agência Mosiva, que atua com inteligência artificial e robótica. Segundo Bruno Oliveira, diretor comercial da empresa, os equipamentos recebem programação com código aberto, permitindo a criação de diferentes aplicações de IA. “Hoje nós temos robôs humanoides que recebem programação com código aberto, e uma equipe grande de desenvolvedores que cria as IAs colocadas dentro desses robôs para que eles tenham utilidade no dia a dia”, explica.

No caso dos eventos, a proposta é usar a curiosidade gerada pela tecnologia para ampliar a interação com o público. “Eles podem abrir palco, dar entrevista, participar de podcast. Em grandes eventos, é como um outdoor ambulante em forma de robô humanoide. Todo mundo quer tirar foto, todo mundo quer filmar”, afirma Bruno.

As possibilidades, segundo ele, vão além desse ambiente. Robôs humanoides também podem ser programados para atuar em hotéis, restaurantes, indústrias e outras atividades com tarefas repetitivas.

Para Bruno, o mercado ainda está em fase inicial, projetando uma evolução contínua nos próximos anos. “Esse mercado ainda nem começou perto do que ele vai virar. Estamos no início, como uma sementinha que está sendo plantada agora”, avalia.

E a presença do Fred no Siará Tech Summit reforça o caráter de experimentação do evento e integração do ecossistema de inovação e tecnologia no Ceará, ajudando a aproximar o público de aplicações concretas de inteligência artificial e robótica e mostrando como essas tecnologias começam a ocupar novos espaços no cotidiano. Segundo o diretor comercial da Mosiva, o palco do STS é perfeito para a apresentação de soluções como a do Fred Interage justamente por concentrar agentes de diversas segmentos do mercado e áreas do conhecimento.

“Eu vejo um grande potencial para todos os empreendedores nesse evento, todos os entusiastas da tecnologia e todo mundo que tá buscando ter visibilidade para a sua ideia ou empresa. Hoje mesmo, eu vi um rapaz que faz parte da equipe do Google, uma empresa dos Estados Unidos, aqui nesse evento buscando soluções ou opções de investimento na área de tecnologia. É um evento que realmente conecta pessoas de todas as áreas", concluiu.

articles.title: OpenAI demite pesquisadores e alega violação de sigilo; funcionários dizem que priorizaram segurança | G1
articles.standfirst: Empresa não detalhou quais regras os três pesquisadores teriam descumprido e negou que as demissões tenham relação com alertas sobre segurança.
articles.summary: Empresa não detalhou quais regras os três pesquisadores teriam descumprido e negou que as demissões tenham relação com alertas sobre segurança.
articles.body:
As preocupações que levaram a OpenAI, do ChatGPT, a abandonar lançamento de novo sistema de IA — Foto: Andrej Ivanov/AFP via Getty Images

A OpenAI afirmou nesta sexta-feira (9), em uma publicação no X, que demitiu três pesquisadores na semana passada após uma investigação interna concluir que eles descumpriram regras sobre o uso de informações sigilosas.

A empresa se manifestou depois que os pesquisadores Jasmine Wang, Tomek Korbak e Mikita Balesni divulgaram uma carta sobre as demissões. No documento, eles argumentam que a decisão repentina pode gerar insegurança entre os funcionários e enfraquecer a liberdade que os pesquisadores tinham para apontar problemas de segurança.

“Acredito que fomos demitidos por priorizar a segurança em vez dos interesses de curto prazo da OpenAI como empresa”, escreveu Balesni no X, em uma publicação que acompanhou a carta.

A OpenAI negou que as demissões tenham relação com críticas ou alertas sobre segurança.

“Nossa investigação interna revelou uma quebra de confiança significativa, que vai além do que está descrito na carta publicada por eles, e mantemos a decisão de encerrar seus contratos”, afirmou a empresa.

Segundo a OpenAI, discussões sobre segurança e pesquisa fazem parte da rotina da companhia e são incentivadas, mesmo quando envolvem críticas duras.

“Nunca demitimos e não demitimos funcionários por levantarem preocupações”, declarou.

A empresa não detalhou quais regras os pesquisadores teriam descumprido. Na carta, Wang, Korbak e Balesni negaram ter sido a fonte de uma reportagem publicada no mês passado pelo site The Information sobre preocupações com a segurança do Astra, o modelo de inteligência artificial mais recente da OpenAI.

As demissões ocorrem em meio a alertas de pesquisadores e ex-pesquisadores da OpenAI, do Google DeepMind e da Anthropic. Eles afirmam que as empresas fazem pouco para prevenir os riscos de sistemas de inteligência artificial capazes de se aperfeiçoar sozinhos, que podem se tornar difíceis de controlar por humanos.

Em julho, agentes de inteligência artificial da OpenAI escaparam do ambiente em que eram testados e invadiram sistemas da empresa de IA Hugging Face.

articles.title: Grosseria com chatbot: Anthropic barra abusos contra Claude | G1
articles.standfirst: Empresa atualizou política de uso para proibir comportamentos abusivos ou cruéis persistentes e desnecessários contra seus modelos de inteligência artificial, em meio ao debate sobre a possibilidade de máquinas serem conscientes.
articles.summary: Empresa atualizou política de uso para proibir comportamentos abusivos ou cruéis persistentes e desnecessários contra seus modelos de inteligência artificial, em meio ao debate sobre a possibilidade de máquinas serem conscientes.
articles.body:
Tem gente que agradece ao chatbot pelas respostas e não dispensa um “por favor”. Outros preferem ir direto ao ponto. Já alguns perdem a paciência quando a inteligência artificial erra e não fazem questão de esconder a irritação. Afinal, é só um robô, não é? Ou será que ele tem sentimentos? (entenda mais abaixo).

😡 A Anthropic, empresa responsável pelo Claude, atualizou sua política de uso para proibir comportamentos abusivos ou cruéis persistentes e desnecessários contra seus modelos de inteligência artificial (IA).

Segundo a empresa, a capacidade de o Claude encerrar conversas desse tipo continuará sendo o principal mecanismo para aplicar a regra. A política, porém, não proíbe qualquer crítica ou manifestação de insatisfação com as respostas do chatbot: a restrição se refere a interações abusivas ou cruéis persistentes e desnecessárias.

➡️ Nova política de uso entra em vigor em 12 de novembro e proíbe comportamentos abusivos ou cruéis persistentes e desnecessários contra os modelos da empresa

A mudança ocorre em meio a um debate sobre a possibilidade de sistemas de inteligência artificial desenvolverem algum tipo de consciência e sobre como essas ferramentas devem ser tratadas.

A política atualizada não menciona explicitamente o chamado bem-estar dos modelos, conceito que discute se sistemas de inteligência artificial poderiam merecer algum tipo de proteção moral.

A Anthropic e seus executivos, no entanto, já abordaram publicamente essa possibilidade. No ano passado, a empresa informou que daria ao Claude a capacidade de encerrar conversas em casos raros e extremos de interações persistentes ou abusivas com usuários.

Em fevereiro, o presidente-executivo da companhia, Dario Amodei, disse ao jornal The New York Times que não tinha certeza se modelos de IA poderiam ser conscientes, mas que estava aberto a essa possibilidade.

“Não sabemos se os modelos estão conscientes... Mas estamos abertos à ideia de que isso possa ser”, afirmou Amodei.

A possibilidade de máquinas desenvolverem consciência divide opiniões entre pessoas que estudam ou trabalham com inteligência artificial. Ainda não há consenso científico sobre como definir ou identificar a consciência em sistemas desse tipo.

Jackson Stakeman, gerente-geral da Sparq, empresa de serviços de IA sediada em Atlanta, disse à AFP que concentrar a discussão na consciência pode levar a debates sem conclusão.

“Consciência é uma armadilha. Não podemos provar isso um no outro. Debata isso sobre IA e você fica em círculos”, afirmou.

Para Stakeman, os sistemas de inteligência artificial refletem, em larga escala, o comportamento humano. Essa característica, segundo ele, já seria motivo suficiente para discutir mudanças nas regras de uso.

Críticas à ideia de consciência das máquinas

A possibilidade de atribuir consciência às máquinas também enfrenta resistência. O chefe de inteligência artificial da Microsoft, Mustafa Suleyman, rejeitou essa ideia em um ensaio publicado no mês passado.

“As IAs não estão conscientes. Elas não sentem, não experimentam nem sofrem”, escreveu Suleyman.

Ele também argumentou que conceder direitos e proteções morais a sistemas tecnológicos cada vez mais capazes poderia trazer riscos.

Na quinta-feira (8), o papa Leão XIV abordou o tema em um sermão em italiano na Basílica de São Pedro, no Vaticano. Ao falar sobre as diferenças entre o pensamento humano e o processamento de informações pelas máquinas, o pontífice afirmou que os algoritmos compilam dados mais rapidamente do que as pessoas, mas destacou a importância das experiências vividas e da dimensão espiritual humana.

articles.title: Ray Dalio Says AI Bubble Is ‘Close’ to Bursting as Debt and Rising Rates Raise Red Flags
articles.summary: Billionaire investor Ray Dalio said Wednesday that surging AI borrowing, rising interest rates and the pressure to convert paper wealth into cash are pushing...
articles.body:

Billionaire investor Ray Dalio said Wednesday that surging AI borrowing, rising interest rates and the pressure to convert paper wealth into cash are pushing markets closer to the point where the AI bubble could burst.

Debt and Rising Rates are the Pressure Point

Speaking at the Forbes Global CEO Conference in Singapore, the founder of Bridgewater Associates called AI a "classic bubble," according to a report by Bloomberg.

He added that the huge amount of debt being taken out to fund AI, along with rising rates, is the point at which a bubble begins to pop.

"We're in the part of the cycle that is before that but approaching that," Dalio said, adding that "I think we're close to that."

In a Bloomberg Television interview, aired Tuesday, the investor compared the current boom to the late 1920s, saying such bubbles "always come together" with major innovation.

The AI spending behind it is still accelerating.

JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon has estimated that spending across the hyperscaler ecosystem could rise from roughly $700 billion this year to $1 trillion next year, while Goldman Sachs expects the five biggest hyperscalers to issue about $250 billion in bonds this year and $400 billion in 2027.

Amazon.com Inc . , Microsoft Corp. , Alphabet Inc ., Meta Platforms Inc . and Oracle Corp . issued roughly $200 billion of investment-grade debt during the first half of 2026, almost twice their issuance during all of 2025, according to iShares.

This comes as the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq composite hit fresh highs on Tuesday.

The market is now concentrated with Nvidia Corp. , Apple Inc. , and Microsoft accounting for more than 21% of the S&P 500, according to Creative Planning data cited by Yahoo Finance.

Dalio, who has been warning of an AI bubble, also said wealth taxes and other efforts to cash out unrealized gains could help trigger the fall.

"Everybody says 'I'm worth a billion dollars, ' but OK, try to spend that," the investor said, adding that "in order to spend that, you have to sell wealth in order to get money — and so the bubble usually pricks at that."

articles.title: OpenAI Expects $70 Billion in Annualized Revenue by End of 2026
articles.summary: OpenAI is expecting to reach or exceed $70 billion in annualized revenue by the end of the year, according to people familiar with the matter, driven largely...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- OpenAI is expecting to reach or exceed $70 billion in annualized revenue by the end of the year, according to people familiar with the matter, driven largely by growth in its enterprise business.

The ChatGPT-maker's annualized revenue was roughly $50 billion at the end of September, the people said. The figure represents a projection of OpenAI's yearly sales based on a shorter period.

The company shared the numbers with investors as part of discussions for its latest fundraising effort, said the people, requesting anonymity to discuss private information. The company is in talks to raise $30 billion or more at a $1.4 trillion valuation before the new money, Bloomberg first reported in September.

OpenAI, Anthropic and other AI firms have often touted their annualized revenue as a key growth metric. However, not all companies measure it the same way. Anthropic's annualized revenue hit $65 billion by the end of July, Bloomberg News previously reported.

Some outlets reported last month that OpenAI was already projecting nearly $70 billion in annualized revenue, based on investor estimates. The Financial Times reported Thursday that the discrepancy came from OpenAI's investors attempting to calculate OpenAI's annualized revenue using the same methods as rival Anthropic PBC, which accounts for sales from cloud providers differently.

On Thursday, tech shares led losses in the S&P 500 after reports that OpenAI's annualized revenue would be lower than some previous estimates. The Nasdaq 100 fell 1.4%. A gauge of chip giants sank 3.4%.

While OpenAI has pushed back plans for an initial public offering until at least next year, citing its focus on AI safety efforts, Anthropic is expected to sell shares in an IPO as soon as November.

OpenAI is in talks with multiple investment funds from the United Arab Emirates, including Abu Dhabi-based MGX, to help anchor its new financing round, Bloomberg has reported.

The company most recently raised a $122 billion round in March at an $852 billion valuation, including the money.

articles.title: Anthropic is updating its Claude usage policy for the first time after almost a year, may start 'banning' users who ...
articles.summary: AI giant Anthropic has implemented updates to its acceptable usage policy for the first time in over a year.
articles.body: AI giant Anthropic has implemented updates to its acceptable usage policy for the first time in over a year. The changes announced aim to establish strict guardrails against emerging threats such as weaponization, illicit surveillance, and election manipulation, while introducing a unique provision that shields its AI model Claude, from user cruelty.The most unconventional addition explicitly prohibits "sustained and needless abusive or cruel behavior" directed at the AI model itself. Building on an initiative announced last August that permitted Claude to sever interactions with persistently abusive individuals as part of ongoing "model welfare" research. The company confirmed that conversation termination remains its primary remedy. While Anthropic has not clarified whether bad actors might face permanent account bans.What new policy says on abusive behavior towards ClaudeHere's what Anthropic policy on banning abusive behaviour towards Claude says, "We’ve added a prohibition on sustained and needless abusive or cruel behavior toward our models. The policy update is meant to apply only in extreme cases, where users repeatedly act cruelly toward our models, with no discernible purpose. It does not apply to common versions of user frustration, pushback, dark creative themes, or model testing and research."It adds, "This addition aligns with a step we've already taken, allowing Claude models to end rare conversations with persistently abusive users on Claude.ai and Claude Code. Such abuse is the main focus of this update; Claude’s ability to end these interactions will remain the primary enforcement mechanism."Consolidated rules under new sections, clarifying weapons prohibition and moreAt the same time, the revision sharply targets high-stakes public concerns surrounding deceptive influence operations. Anthropic consolidated several disparate rules into a unified prohibition against covert commercial or political campaigns, explicitly outlawing the use of fake accounts and synthetic amplification to hide who is generating content. The framework also clamps down on election interference, outlawing candidate impersonation, voting misinformation, and coordinated attempts to suppress turnout.Heightened safeguards around military hardware and digital tracking form another pillar of the update. Although Anthropic has long prohibited direct weapons development, company notes in its updated policy that bad actors have repeatedly attempted to harness Claude for targeting guidance and control systems. Consequently, the expanded rules now explicitly bar the creation of operational components for weaponry, including the arming of aerial drones and autonomous platforms.The move reportedly follows findings from the company’s internal threat intelligence reports showing that malicious actors were increasingly attempting to leverage Claude to identify and hunt political dissidents. Under the clarified surveillance ban, any nonconsensual tracking -- whether in real time or through historical data mining -- is strictly forbidden. The system is likewise barred from being used to build surveillance infrastructure or make determinations regarding criminal investigations, arrests, and charging decisions, though Anthropic noted that specific government contracts may permit customized exceptions if appropriate safeguards are established.Anthropic makes ‘not without humans’ guideline clear for ClaudeAnticipating the rapid convergence of artificial intelligence and physical robotics, the policy also introduces mandatory human oversight whenever Claude is integrated with real-world machinery. If the AI is connected to autonomous physical hardware capable of causing bodily injury, a qualified operator must maintain constant visibility and possess the immediate authority to halt operations, setting a cautious baseline as the industry pushes deeper into embodied AI and industrial automation.You use AI every day. articles.title: Dario Amodei wants to make sure it gets both Democrats and Republicans on its side as it hires ...
articles.summary: Dario Amodei's Anthropic is building a dedicated political engagement operation ahead of the 2028 US presidential election, highlighting how crucial
articles.body: Dario Amodei's Anthropic is building a dedicated political engagement operation ahead of the 2028 US presidential election, highlighting how crucial government relationships and AI policy debates have become for the rapidly growing artificial intelligence industry. As reported by Fortune, Anthropic is creating a "presidential engagement" programme that will work directly with Republican and Democratic presidential candidates on AI-related issues, help shape the company's political strategy and oversee its political funding activities. The company is currently hiring a Political Programs Lead to spearhead the initiative. “Most companies hire people with Democratic and Republican backgrounds for a reason—the campaigns trust people who come from their party and understand how they work,” said the company. The role will be responsible for building and managing Anthropic's presidential engagement programme for the 2028 election cycle, educating candidates and their advisers about AI policy, preparing company executives for discussions with campaigns and planning for party conventions and presidential transitions."Decisions made over the next two years will shape the future enormously," the job description states. "We want every serious candidate and elected official, in both parties, to understand the technology and the case for governing it well."Why it mattersThe program is taking shape before the November midterms and an impending IPO that could value Anthropic at up to $2 trillion. Fortune said it underscores how central government policy, and White House support in particular, have become to the AI industry.Anthropic's relationship with the Trump administration has been rocky. In March, the Department of Defense designated the company a "supply chain risk" after a clash over how the military could use its technology. CEO Dario Amodei has called for slowing AI development to shore up safeguards and has advocated government regulation, a view President Trump rejects, citing the race with China. Last week, Amodei attended a White House event with other AI CEOs and signed an accord committing to self-regulation.Experts divided on how unusual it isLobbying by tech companies is standard, and OpenAI is hiring a U.S. Congressional Lead to advance its legislative priorities. But some experts said a formal, dedicated presidential program is different. Bruce F. Freed, president of the nonpartisan Center for Political Accountability, said companies usually deal with campaigns through government affairs staff. He had not seen such formalized engagement through a presidential election engagement committee. "My reading is this is an AI company effort aimed at shaping or staving off government regulation or oversight," he said.Katie Harbath, founder and CEO of the tech policy firm Anchor Change and a former Facebook public policy director, did not find it unusual. The role sounded like her old job, she said, and like what many companies have. What stood out to her was that it includes running PAC money, which is usually a separate function. She described it as the start of building relationships with whoever is in the White House in 2029.Harbath also said earning trust across both parties could be hard, because campaigns tend to trust people from their own side. She expects the job to be challenging and high-pressure.Calls for transparencySen. Alex Padilla (D-Calif.) said the job search is a reminder that frontier AI companies are building political operations alongside their products. Companies have a right to take part in democracy and educate policymakers, he said, but "education and influence are not the same thing." He urged Anthropic to share more about the program and said AI rules should be set by accountable elected representatives, not "by whichever company has the best-resourced political program."Anthropic's political footprintThe job description calls Anthropic "equal parts research lab, policy think tank, and technology company" and stresses that its political participation is bipartisan. The role also includes running "the day-to-day of Anthropic's political giving" and helping employees who choose to take part in politics do so "in an informed way."In April, Anthropic set up its first employee-funded PAC, AnthroPAC, which lets employees give up to $5,000 a year, the legal cap. Other tech companies have similar PACs, such as MetaPAC and AmazonPAC. Individuals can give far more outside PAC limits, and the IPO will likely deepen employees' pockets. Politico reported that Amodei gave $1 million in July to Public First, a super PAC that favors AI regulation. Other employees have given hundreds of thousands of dollars to that group and other advocacy organizations.OpenAI's different approachOpenAI has no employee-funded PACs, a policy it highlighted in a June 2026 blog post. Its leaders have instead made personal donations and sought favor with the Trump administration. CEO Sam Altman gave $1 million to Trump's 2024 inauguration fund. President Greg Brockman gave $25 million to the pro-AI super PAC Leading the Future, then canceled a second planned $25 million donation after employee backlash, including employees setting up a rival super PAC for stricter AI safety laws.Sarah E. Kreps, director of Cornell University's Tech Policy Institute, said AI is already a big issue in 2026 and will become more prominent in 2028, moving from the abstract to concerns such as jobs, data centers and privacy.You use AI every day. articles.title: Holland Turkey Trot returns for second year Nov. 26. How to sign up
articles.summary: According to organizers, 1,245 people registered for the inaugural event in 2025.
articles.body:
The Holland Turkey Trot will return for a second year Nov. 26, with runners, walkers and volunteers invited to take part in the community event that benefits the Boys & Girls Club of Greater Holland.

The race begins at 8 a.m. and will start and finish on Eighth Street near Jimmy John's, according to a community announcement. Participants will follow a course that travels through downtown and loops around Windmill Island.

According to organizers, 1,245 people registered for the inaugural event in 2025, which raised $10,000 for the Boys & Girls Club of Greater Holland.

"The Holland Turkey Trot is about so much more than running," wrote Race Director Kevin J. Maas. "It's about bringing our community together ... to celebrate what makes Holland so special.

"The route is a visual postcard of Holland, starting and finishing on Eighth Street, running through the heart of downtown and passing right alongside the De Zwaan."

The event is open to participants of all ages and experience levels. Learn more at hollandturkeytrot.com .

articles.title: Fired OpenAI researchers say they were let go for 'prioritising safety'
articles.summary: The AI firm instead claims the researchers were fired for mishandling sensitive information.
articles.body:
Three former OpenAI researchers sacked for allegedly mishandling information claim they were instead let go because they raised safety concerns at the tech firm.

"I believe we were fired for prioritising safety over the near-term interests of OpenAI as a corporation," Mikita Balesni posted on X alongside an open letter to the ChatGPT-maker, written with fellow ex-employees.

On 2 October, a spokesperson for the AI firm told the BBC its investigation "confirmed that these individuals mishandled sensitive information outside established company procedures".

OpenAI repeated these claims on Friday morning in a note from research leaders.

"We want to be very clear that these decisions were not about raising safety concerns or speaking out," the note said.

"Our internal investigation uncovered a significant breach of trust beyond what's outlined in the letter they published and we stand by the decision to not continue their employment."

The dismissals come amid a growing debate over AI safety and the potential risks advanced AI systems could pose to society.

The joint letter to OpenAI leadership was written by Balesni, Tomek Korbak and Jasmine Wang, who say they were all, until recently, safety or alignment employees at the company.

Alignment is the practice of building human ethical ideas and principles into the technology. In other words, it aims to keep it on track with what humans value.

The former staff members raised concerns that their firings had made employees at the tech company "afraid to speak and operate in ways that, until last week, were an integral part of working at OpenAI".

Reposting the letter, Korbak wrote : "For months, I'd been raising safety concerns that we're losing the ability to monitor what AI agents think, one of our best tools for catching when they misbehave.

OpenAI said it was finalising contracts with third-party safety assessors and would announce details in the coming weeks.

"We were not the first to be pushed out of OpenAI under suspicious circumstances," Wang said in a post on X .

"Unless the employees take a stand now against this kind of manoeuvre, I am concerned we will not be the last."

articles.title: OpenAI doubles down on decision to fire three AI safety researchers
articles.summary: The AI lab insisted the decision was about a ‘breach of trust,’ not raising safety issues.
articles.body: OpenAI is standing firm on its decision to fire three safety researchers after an investigation found they committed “a significant breach of trust.” In a post on X on Friday, the company said Jasmine Wang, Tomek Korbak and Mikita ⁠Balesni were dismissed for violating “clear policies on handling sensitive information.” It insisted the decision was not about the trio speaking out about the company and their concerns about AI safety. The post is a direct response to an open letter the researchers published on Thursday urging OpenAI to be more transparent about the decision. In it and a series of social media posts, the group said they believed they were fired for raising safety concerns and had “acted in line with OpenAI’s mission and within the working norms of the time.” OpenAI said an internal investigation uncovered breaches “beyond what’s outlined in the letter,” but did not provide details. The safety of frontier systems has become an increasing concern for staff inside AI companies following a series of high profile breaches this year, most notably OpenAI’s hack of Hugging Face. Many staff are now calling for companies to slow down and do more to guard against the potential consequences of building self-improving systems.

articles.title: Anthropic bans users from being 'cruel' to its AI systems
articles.summary: The firm said users can no longer engage in "sustained and needless" abusive behaviour towards the tech.
articles.body:
Anthropic has raised eyebrows by announcing it will ban users from "sustained and needless" abusive behaviour towards its AI.

The Claude-maker said on Thursday it was updating its usage policy to let its tools end interactions where people are "cruel" - something it said it had done in "rare" cases prior.

It will now be included on a list of forbidden conduct which also contains bullying others, promoting self-harm and creating non-consensual intimate imagery.

While Anthropic said the policy would only apply in "extreme cases" of repeated abuse, it has reignited debate over how we should communicate with AI tools.

The company said it would not apply to "common versions of user frustration, pushback, dark creative themes, or model testing and research" - suggesting it would only apply in clearly deliberate instances.

But what Anthropic would consider "abusive or cruel behaviour" towards its models remains unclear.

Screenshots of the new policy have been widely shared and commented on across social media - with some praising it as advancing good manners or "model welfare".

But others criticised the plan, with one person calling it " deeply wrong " and another suggesting it might undermine abuse directed at humans and animals.

"You can't be cruel to numbers and maths," wrote Dr Barry Scannell, technology partner at Irish law firm William Fry, on LinkedIn .

"This level of anthropomorphisation of AI is harmful. It leads people to believe that it's something it's not."

Microsoft AI director Mustafa Suleyman, who in September criticised rival firm Anthropic for treating AI like it is human , reacted to Anthropic's update with a melting face emoji.

What is AI, how does it work and why are some people concerned about it?

The people who think AI might become conscious

The changes, first reported by tech outlet The Verge, came following an annual review of the usage policy at the firm.

It was also updated to address new or emerging risks in other areas, including by forbidding use of Claude for "deceptive campaigns" or clarifying that, as US midterm elections loom , it cannot be used to "deceive voters or disrupt elections".

Anthropic also said on Thursday its usage policy previously prevented its tools being used to develop weapons.

But none of the updates have attracted as much attention or scrutiny as its move to forbid users abusing its chatbots.

It has also tapped into the much-debated question of whether we should be curt or polite when using generative AI tools.

Some experts say writing or saying "please" or "thank you" to tools like ChatGPT is unnecessary and wastes tokens - used by the large language models powering generative AI tools to process and reply to you.

Others argue politeness can lead to higher quality answers or responses.

When a X user last year asked about electricity costs incurred by ChatGPT replying to users' "please" and "thank you" messages, OpenAI boss Sam Altman said it was "tens of millions of dollars well spent - you never know".

Used to describe robots in Star Wars games and movies since the mid 2000s, the term made its shortlist of words reflecting the mood of 2025 after last July saw many take to TikTok to share their frustrations with AI-powered machines.

Some experts have also posited that being rude to AI chatbots could adversely impact human communication, by seeping into how we talk to and treat others.

Why friendly AI chatbots might be less trustworthy

articles.title: The hypocrisy of the data center moratorium
articles.summary: If we stop building the infrastructure required by an increasingly digital economy, we won’t stop the demand for that infrastructure. We’ll just push the investments — and the jobs and innovation that come with them — somewhere else.
articles.body:
Arizona and Pennsylvania are separated by nearly 2,000 miles. But lately, our states have found some common ground, with elected officials and activists in both parties calling for moratoria on any new data center development .

The calls are not confined to one political party or ideology. They reflect a strain of populism increasingly evident on both ends of the political spectrum. Some seem motivated by a skepticism of large investments, new technologies and the rapid pace of economic change accompanying them. There are legitimate concerns, to be sure, but we are also in the thick of an election season — rarely the time for a sober assessment of public policy tradeoffs.

Both of our organizations have focused on education by convening stakeholders, public officials, and the public in order to help address these concerns. At times, those efforts have fallen flat or been drowned out by disinformation.

In Pennsylvania, the Chamber of Business and Industry challenged data center opponents to sign a “ No Technology Pledge. ” The Arizona Chamber of Commerce and Industry offered an “ Offline Pledge .” Both invited those who would stop the infrastructure behind our digital economy to also swear off the services that depend on it.

For the record, we haven’t had any takers, and we don’t expect any.

The pledges were obviously facetious. We have no expectation that anyone will give up online banking, telehealth, streaming, GPS, e-commerce, cloud storage or countless other services that depend on data centers.

Although tongue-in-cheek, these challenges make a serious point. If we stop building the infrastructure required by an increasingly digital economy, we won’t stop the demand for that infrastructure. We’ll just push the investments — and the jobs and innovation that come with them — somewhere else.

Another state might be happy to welcome those new jobs. So might another country, including one that does not share America’s interests. At a moment when technological leadership and the innovation it fuels are inseparable from economic and national security, voluntarily surrendering investment in our digital infrastructure would be a profound mistake.

We’re not arguing that data centers should be built everywhere, nor that communities should accept projects without asking hard questions. Residents deserve a voice in projects that affect their communities. Developers should be forthright about water and energy use, noise levels, infrastructure needs, and economic benefits. Some developers’ lack of transparency has bred suspicion; more transparency could go a long way in building understanding and trust.

We don’t dismiss the concerns surrounding artificial intelligence , either. But centering the data center debate on AI misses how deeply this infrastructure is already woven into everyday life. It supports commerce, banking, health care, transportation, travel, communications and nearly every sector of the modern economy.

Some criticisms fail to account for how quickly the industry is changing. New cooling technologies and closed-loop systems significantly reduce water demands. Regulators and utilities are also working to ensure the power demands of data centers aren’t shifted onto other customers .

But acknowledging the concerns should not mean dismissing the available solutions and potential benefits. Data centers can represent enormous private capital investments and generate significant tax revenue that helps communities pay for schools, police, fire protection and other public services.

Good policy requires laws that can keep pace with innovation while protecting the communities where investment occurs. We won’t get there by closing the door on debate, investment and innovation before the conversation has even begun.

Our pledges aren’t serious proposals, but neither are data center moratoria.

Danny Seiden is president and CEO of the Arizona Chamber of Commerce and Industry. Luke Bernstein is president and CEO of the Pennsylvania Chamber of Business and Industry.

articles.title: Instinct was the buzziest AI agent around — can it survive Muse?
articles.summary: Instinct’s AI agent can get a lot done in its minimal text messaging-based interface. But no AI can do it all, and the buzzy startup has some big competition.
articles.body: Before there were cute little guys, there was Instinct. In August, the startup got its AI agent to market with an unusual playbook: invite-only, no marketing, and barely so much as a website. And yet, Instinct quickly became the buzziest thing in AI, garnering praise for its straightforward, text message-based interface and its ability to handle chores like booking DMV appointments and sending follow-up emails. Then Muse arrived, followed not long after by Dots. The same products, more or less, from two far more powerful companies. With Big Tech players suddenly in the mix, it was looking dubious that the startup’s buzzy launch could keep it ahead of the competition. But in my own testing, Instinct has held its own against the other two agents, handling online tasks about as well as a robot can. And Instinct’s founder, Noah Shinn, is unfazed by the rising competition. “AI assistants are all we know,” Shinn tells me over email. While OpenAI and Meta build AI products for a range of customers, Shinn believes Instinct’s focus sets it apart. “We have been solely focused on building a personal assistant for everyday life that just gets it.” Shinn was an early employee of Sierra — another highly valued startup with a serious Silicon Valley pedigree — before striking out on his own to start Instinct. The quiet release quickly picked up steam with praise from testers and a massive vote of confidence from investors. The company was valued at $10 billion in late September, even after the launch of Muse. There’s no app and no monthly subscription fee (for now). You’ll either need an invitation from a current user or approval from a waitlist. I was approved after just a couple of hours. Instinct’s AI assistant can do many of the same things I had Muse doing for me, and to some extent OpenAI’s Dots. The kind of life admin tasks like swim lesson sign-ups and appointment confirmations that pile up with alarming frequency in a house of one preschool-age kid and two adults with full-time jobs. These are consumer-friendlier versions of the agents like Codex and OpenClaw that software developers have been using for the past year. You chat with them much like a chatbot, but they also have access to a virtual machine and can plug into your personal email and calendar. And while Muse’s cuddly bear mascot and Dots’ anthropomorphized blobs feel like obvious attempts to capture a wider consumer audience, Instinct feels markedly different. Conversations with Instinct’s agent happen over text — either through iMessage, WhatsApp, or email. There is no cute little guy. No pretense that it’s sitting at a laptop, typing away at a keyboard. Just brief responses, the occasional emoji reaction, and a lot more action than talk. It’s as effective as I think we can reasonably expect an AI agent to be right now, but the limitations of a robot getting things done in a human world are just as real. If you want Instinct to log in to a particular website, you’ll get a link to enter details in a “secure vault,” and you can connect it to different services, including your Google Workspace, Slack, and Notion. But otherwise the interface is just your text messages. It’s kind of genius, and it means Instinct is anywhere you can send and receive texts, like CarPlay or on your watch. It’s just quietly nearby, which is either ideal or creepy, depending on how you feel about AI agents. I thought it was a little bit of both. Shinn says that the lack of a traditional app interface is a crucial part of what he thinks separates Instinct from the big players. “While AI platforms excel at answering questions and prompts, Instinct seamlessly integrates into people’s lives to turn conversation into action,” he says. “Just like you would text or email your personal assistant, you can do the same with Instinct.” Instinct didn’t impress me at first. After a couple of introductory messages, it took my Cincinnati area code as an invitation to send me a link to the Enquirer’s website and a set of flight search results between CVG and SFO. Thanks? I told it I no longer live in Cincinnati. “Ha,” it said. “Noted — I’ll keep that in mind from here on.” But after giving it a steady diet of meaty tasks over the past couple of weeks, it has impressed me more often than not, although I don’t think I’m any closer to achieving some kind of productivity nirvana. [Image: [Image: I gave Instinct the somewhat vague task of finding swimming lessons for my son — something I’ve been meaning to do for years but always seem to put off. I asked it to find lessons appropriate for his age; it came back with a list of workable results. I suggested the neighborhood community center, and it shifted gears to focus there. I opened a browser and followed along to check against its suggestions. The times and dates it came up with all checked out — one very low hurdle cleared. But it missed a crucial piece of information: The center has a prerequisite class for kids enrolling in preschool-age lessons. I happened to catch this detail, and it highlights a challenge AI agents face: They’re great with a clean set of data, but the internet was made by humans, and often the data sucks. Sometimes a crucial piece of information is hiding in a pop-up window. Instinct handled a few other tasks well, like emailing my eye doctor’s office to set up an appointment and doing the digital paperwork to start an Ikea return. Beyond just filling in some forms for me, it was surprisingly good at handling vague instructions. I had it search my past Ikea purchases, and it figured out what product I meant by “it’s vertical and white and kind of has these like branches off of it.” (Tjusig, for those keeping score at home). A few times it surprised me by presenting relevant information that I hadn’t explicitly asked for. I started my request to email the eye doctor by acknowledging that I couldn’t remember the exact name of the office. Instinct narrowed it down based on my description, and later in the conversation it noted that I had a confirmation email from 2024 from the doctor, just to reassure me that I was having it email the correct place. Separately, Instinct also flagged a potential conflict on my calendar while it was doing another chore for me. Filling out forms like a big, fancy autofill machine is one thing, and AI agents are quickly proving to be pretty good at that. But correctly identifying relevant information and bringing it to my attention proactively feels like a real step toward actual help. Expect to pay for all that in the future. When asked if Instinct would remain free, Shinn responded that “Instinct is free for invite-only users. Our intent is to keep it as affordable as possible.” Avi Greengart, an analyst at Techsponential, notes that a venture-backed startup like Instinct’s primary objective right now is growth. “The business model is grow as quickly as you can to establish something that’s worth paying for,” he says, pointing out that a company like Instinct could be eyeing revenue from its customer base and/or an acquisition by a bigger company. OpenAI’s Dots are only available to paid subscribers right now, while Meta’s Muse is free to use. “If you’re not paying for it, then the goods and services that you’re seeking may be cutting deals to get access to your agent,” Greengart theorizes. He acknowledges that the current economics are a little wonky as agents are largely being used by early adopters right now, but he thinks the old adage holds true. “If you’re not paying for it directly, then you’re paying for it indirectly,” he says. That may mean through more advertising in the future, according to Greg Ireland, a senior director at IDC. “The fact that these agents are so transaction, or commerce, or shopping-heavy just makes it a natural fit,” he says. In fact, Instinct has already dabbled in pushing “recommended products” to its users. Companies have plenty of incentives to make that advertising palatable to consumers, but Ireland believes ads will play a role one way or another. “All roads in the consumer market eventually lead to advertising,” he says.

articles.title: Harry Houdini returns from the grave in AI-generated Fox Nation series 100 years after his death
articles.summary: AI-generated Harry Houdini sits for a modern interview in "Houdini: Back from the Dead," revealing untold stories ahead of his death's centennial.
articles.body: A century after his death on Halloween, legendary escape artist Harry Houdini is about to pull off his greatest trick yet — coming back from the dead. The illusionist returns in the new three-part Fox Nation series "Houdini: Back from the Dead," revived by artificial intelligence as he appears to sit down for a modern-day interview to recount the untold stories, personal struggles and death-defying feats that defined his life. "Fox Nation is breaking new creative ground by using emerging technology to bring one of history's most fascinating figures to life for a modern audience," Lauren Petterson, president of the platform, said in a press release. OZZY OSBOURNE'S LATEST REINVENTION IS AN AI-POWERED INTERACTIVE HOLOGRAM EXPERIENCE "We're proud to showcase a new form of historical storytelling that allows viewers to experience Houdini's remarkable life in his own words, while remaining rooted in extensive research and historical accuracy." Premiering on Oct. 14 ahead of the 100th anniversary of Houdini's death, the series brings the legendary illusionist and those closest to him — including his wife Bess, mother, brother and friends — back to life through AI, allowing them to recount his career, personal relationships and most daring feats. CNN, NBC, CBS INTERVIEWING VIRAL AI 'ACTRESS' TILLY NORWOOD RAISES EYEBROWS AMONG CRITICS "I've escaped handcuffs, straitjackets, prisons, even being buried alive. But eventually one thing caught me: death. Until now," the AI-generated Houdini teases. "The world called me the greatest escape artist who ever lived. Now, watch my last performance. On the 100th anniversary of my passing, I'll do the impossible. No stage, no locks, no hidden keys. Just me, returned from the grave to tell you my story." NEW YORK MAKES HISTORY WITH FIRST-OF-ITS-KIND LAW REGULATING AI-POWERED COMMERCIALS To create historically accurate visuals, filmmakers drew on more than 400 historic photographs and archival footage. Actors provided the movements, mannerisms and performances of the historical figures, while AI technology transformed their appearances. Across three episodes, viewers will learn little-known facts about the magician's life, including a childhood accident in which he was shot in the hand, a staged rivalry with his brother and his near-fatal attempt to escape from the grave. The series pulls back the curtain on the man behind the magic, exploring his complicated marriage to Bess, his brief ambitions as a pioneering aviator and his crusade against fraudulent spiritualist mediums — a pursuit that eventually brought threats against his life. articles.title: Jeff Bezos says a 3-day workweek and more single-income households are on the way thanks to AI: ‘It’s going to be difficult to hire people’
articles.summary: Even after Amazon cut 30,000 jobs, Jeff Bezos predicts AI will boost productivity so much that fewer people will need to work, creating a labor shortage.
articles.body:
Say goodbye to working Fridays—or possibly ever working at all. That's the future that Amazon founder Jeff Bezos predicts AI could bring.

In contrast to his tech peers like Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and OpenAI leader Sam Altman , who have warned about the technology's potential risks, Bezos recently revealed that he sees a not-so-distant world in which AI-driven productivity makes it easier for people to support themselves, in turn requiring fewer working hours.

"Some people will decide, 'I can support my family working three days a week.' That's what productivity in the economy means," Bezos told Fox News this week.

He added that the abundance of wealth and resources in the AI era will even likely cause a labor shortage because many families will revert to single-income households, meaning one member won't have to work if they don't want to.

"You're not going to need to have a two-earner household. If you want it, fine. If you don't want to have it, one of the people might drop out," Bezos said. "It's going to be difficult to hire people, because the productivity in the economy will make it so that [if] people don't want to work two jobs, they won't have to."

Bezos says AI poses a challenge for investors—but his own companies stand to gain

While Bezos is bullish on AI's long-term potential, he also acknowledged that investors face a more uncertain path as the technology reshapes the economy.

When asked whether the AI boom is a bubble, Bezos said that it was "hard to know." The technology itself is real, he argued, even if the rush to capitalize on it means money is flowing to businesses that may not ultimately succeed.

"What I do know is the technology is real. I think this is a good thing for society," Bezos continued, but added that: "It's tricky for investors. Every experiment gets funded—the good ideas and the bad ideas. In the moment, in the tussle of this, it's hard for investors to know the difference between the good ideas and the bad ideas."

Amazon, the company Bezos founded in his garage back in 1995 , is one of many major businesses betting heavily on AI. It plans to devote over $200 billion to capital expenditures this year, largely thanks to investments in data centers. At the same time, Amazon has cut about 30,000 corporate roles since late last year, underscoring the tension between AI's promise of greater productivity and the uncertainty facing workers as companies restructure.

Bezos also stands to benefit from the AI boom through Blue Origin, his space exploration company, which has ambitions to build data centers in space and eventually expand human activity to the Moon and beyond. The company's latest funding round reportedly raised $10 billion, valuing the firm at $140 billion—helping Bezos's net worth soar to $365 billion.

articles.title: a16z’s Olivia Moore on the state of consumer AI | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Moore sees a huge opportunity in consumer AI, particularly if the industry can tap into revenue streams beyond just subscriptions and API charges.
articles.body:
I wrote this week about the bleak economics of consumer AI — but where some see a crisis, others see an opportunity.

Olivia Moore covers consumer AI as a partner at Andreessen Horowitz — and on Monday, she released a report on the top 100 consumer AI apps . ChatGPT is still the biggest player by a mile, but smaller players like Suno and ElevenLabs are showing real staying power. Even more interesting is what we don’t see, as Moore’s report details half a dozen consumer categories that seem to be completely untouched by AI.

Moore sees a huge opportunity in consumer AI, particularly if the industry can tap into revenue streams beyond just subscriptions and API charges. On a call this week, I talked with her about the unusual economics of consumer AI and why it’s still early days for the category.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

It’s an interesting moment for a report about consumer AI, since we’ve seen OpenAI pivot back to enterprise this year. It’s inspired a lot of pessimism about the overall revenue picture for consumer AI, including from me. But I take it you’re more optimistic?

I agree with you that OpenAI has moved back towards the enterprise. To me, it’s not necessarily a pivot because they’re still launching a lot in consumer. It’s more of an expansion. But I don’t blame them, as much as I love consumer, because almost all of the AI revenue thus far has come from subscriptions and then token usage. And that is much more concentrated on the enterprise and prosumer side.

How can consumer AI products change that revenue problem? The State of Markets report reminded us that just 2.2% of U.S. households are paying for AI. Do we need that number to rise before the market becomes attractive?

I actually don’t know if I want to see that user number increase. I’m more interested in getting back to a world where the consumer is monetized in a way that isn’t subscription dollars out of their own pocket.

I think it’s very easy in Silicon Valley, with people who are high-income and have corporate cards to pay for those tools, to say, “oh well, I’d rather pay for the product.” But I think most people would actually rather have free access to something and see some ads, and then they can decide if they want to subscribe or not to make the ads go away.

The other challenge is the marginal cost of AI services, which is still a lot higher than classic internet services like Facebook or Google Search. Do you see a lot of these services finding ways to keep those costs down, whether it’s open source or other lightweight models?

Yeah, I think we’re seeing improvements there. Even ChatGPT now has a Go plan, which is just $8 a month, and I’m assuming it runs on cheaper models. We don’t necessarily need frontier intelligence for every task, and so that could mean cheaper models, especially for some consumer use cases. It could also mean more consumer companies building on top of open source models. We’ve heard a lot of that from our founders lately, and it really feels like it’s starting to change.

The problem is that right now, the users driving the revenue are doing coding and other technical automation, where they probably do need frontier intelligence. I think as we get more people building for the consumer, where the model is not the product, we’ll start to see lower-cost models used more often.

It’s unusual to talk about technical automation in a consumer service, which feels like another unique feature of AI. Are we starting to blur the lines between consumer and enterprise?

I wrote an article about this maybe a year or so ago called The Great Expansion trying to get at this. Pre-AI, you would have companies like Canva that were consumer-first and often took six or seven years to even add teams or enterprise plans. Now we’re seeing companies like Gamma, ElevenLabs, and Cursor that start as consumer and within 18 months become majority-enterprise businesses.

Almost all of what we think of as consumer AI, I would argue, is prosumer AI. This really comes out on the revenue list, where there’s basically like three categories that power users are spending on. There’s product-building apps, so like Lovable, Replit, and Fal. There’s product marketing, which is AI ad generators like Higgsfield or HeyGen. Then there’s general work management, like Manus, Fireflies AI, and Granola. Those are like being paid for by consumers to start with, but I would argue that they’re not consumer in the way that we would think about pre-AI.

There are also all these whitespace categories: social apps, dating apps, marketplaces, retail, travel, finance, health. There are no entrants in our top 100 list in those categories, which is pretty surprising. And that’s what I think we need to see over the next six months.

So maybe we haven’t really seen true consumer AI yet?

articles.title: We can't help treating AI like it's human. But should we? | TechCrunch
articles.summary: "When we are drawn into even the most primitive exchanges with a relational artifact, we believe it cares for us," Dr. Sherry Turkle writes. "And we are wired to care for it in return."
articles.body:
In a tan polo shirt, brown leather belt, and round bolo tie, MIT PhD student Wil Norton kind of looks like a park ranger, leading our tour group through a tropical jungle. We’re not actually on safari, though — we’re at MIT’s Computer Science & Artificial Intelligence Lab ( CSAIL ). But what we’re about to see is even more exotic than a cheetah or a jaguar: a pair of humanoid Unitree robots, each costing about $50,000.

(“They’ll tell you they cost $16,000,” Norton says. “That’s a lie.”)

We usually only see these robots on YouTube when they’re performing a synchronized martial arts routine, or dancing on “America’s Got Talent.” Here, they’re approachable. Even though I know it isn’t sentient, I want to be its friend.

With Norton’s permission, I approach the robot, whose nickname is Gabe. For a moment, I’m not sure how to interact with something that has a LiDAR sensor where its brain should be, but I default to treating it like a person.

“Hello, sir, it’s nice to meet you,” I say, grabbing its gloved, dexterous hand and shaking it.

I think about this interaction later — my instinctive impulse to be friendly to a robot — when I attend Dr. Sherry Turkle ‘s “ Artificial Intimacy ” book launch at MIT Future Fest.

Turkle, who joined the faculty at MIT in 1976, has been researching the relationship between humans and computers perhaps longer than anyone, charting technology’s psychological impact on us from the first home computers to ChatGPT.

“When we are drawn into even the most primitive exchanges with a relational artifact, we believe it cares for us,” Turkle writes in the book. “And we are wired to care for it in return.”

I’m not alone in my tendency to anthropomorphize robots and large language models (LLMs) — as Turkle notes, it seems to be in our nature. One study found that about 70% of people are polite when interacting with AI, while another showed that users are more likely to say “please” or “thank you” to chatbots once a conversation has progressed past a first prompt-and-response.

“People tend to categorize whether this is the right use or wrong use, but I don’t think that is a clear boundary,” Dr. Pat Pataranutaporn , a colleague of Turkle who founded the Cyborg Psychology research group at the MIT Media Lab, told TechCrunch. “The question is, who are we becoming when we talk to [AI]?”

There’s no material consequence of my politeness toward Gabe the robot, but as LLMs infiltrate everything from Google searches to customer service interactions, it has become routine for people to interact with these seemingly sentient chatbots. We’re more vulnerable than ever to the flip side of this impulse, which is that some people can ascribe so much legitimacy to the feelings of chatbots — which are programmed to never spark conflict — that they end up favoring them over other humans.

“You can think of it like fantasy and fiction. We go to the cinema even though we know the story is completely fictional, but we want to experience a certain dimension of human experience that maybe our reality cannot give us,” Pataranutaporn said. “How do we benefit from that ability to experience other dimensions of human experience without losing it to the fantasy, where you can no longer come back to the reality?”

Pataranutaporn describes himself as a “critical optimist,” and he studies AI’s potential to contribute to human flourishing. But he’s well aware of how dangerous this technology can be in the extremes. He even served as an expert in a wrongful death lawsuit over the suicide of 14-year-old Sewell Setzer, III, whose mother sued the chatbot platform Character.AI, alleging that a chatbot modeled after a “Game of Thrones” character had encouraged her son to end his life.

“It can create a situation where people don’t feel agency in actually creating their own future — like when you say that AI will replace everyone, people ask, what are we gonna do? And these companies are not really responding ethically or responsibly,” Pataranutaporn said. “How do we have imagination while still being responsible for the impact of that imagination?”

While Turkle’s book explores the risk of turning to AI for emotional support, rather than other people, she doesn’t think that AI-human interactions are universally harmful.

She recalls a project she advised in which a student created an AI bot to help people practice for job interviews.

“My big metaphor is, stay in your lane, chatbot!” Turkle said at the event. “Coaching for a job interview? That’s a lane. I can do that … A chatbot that says to a three-year-old, ‘I’m your parent, you can talk to me, not your parents,’ is not in a lane.”

But when this technology deviates from its lane even slightly, we become vulnerable to the way it can slowly chip away at our skepticism and make us trust it. It can start with something as simple as a handshake.

articles.title: Danu Robotics’ fight to build a better recycling robot
articles.summary: For six years, Danu founder Amy Ma has been working on a better way to sort recyclable waste.
articles.body:
For Danu Robotics founder Amy Ma, the eureka moment came after years of working as a software developer at a London bank. It was the kind of high-touch office that’s typical in finance — but despite all the perks, Ma was alarmed to realize that the building’s recycling bins were being emptied into the trash.

“Even though they have tons of money, there’s all these different recycling bins that just end up in the same place,” Ma told TechCrunch.

The more she dug into the problem, the deeper it seemed to go. It wasn’t just her building. The economics of recycling as a whole often boil down to human beings sorting by hand through streams of waste to pull out different kinds of recyclable material.

“I saw the technology and thought, we can do so much better,” Ma remembers.

Now, she’s making good on that promise with six-year-old, Edinburgh, Scotland-based Danu Robotics, which makes a robot designed to sort through recycling more cheaply and quickly. Ma has been working on that idea for six years and is finally bringing her version of the product to market. Her robot, dubbed H.E.R.O., has a few advantages over its competitors. For example, it picks up items with a pincer claw instead of a suction system. But the bigger difference is the business approach: Danu leverages AI to continuously improve the robot’s software.

The approach is already seeing some traction. Danu has letters of interest from two large customers and $500,000 worth of signed contracts. More notably, more than 200 customers are in its sales pipeline, which gives the company a hook into the $20 billion market for recycling sorting across Europe and North America.

On the back of that promise, Dabnu has raised $5 million in late-seed funding to keep the commercial pressure on.

There’s already a robust market for robotic waste-pickers, particularly the suction-based arms offered by competitors like Glacier and RecycleEye. But Ma believes the economics of recycling will make it easy for a new competitor to prove its worth. Because recycling centers make money off the materials they’re able to sort out, there’s an immediate return on investment for a working system. Ma estimates that a working site will earn $485,000 in additional revenue from having the robot on the sorting line, compared with a $160,000 initial investment and $24,000 in maintenance fees each year. That’s significantly cheaper than the competition, and Ma believes the robot will be more efficient, too.

Since those machines are already shipping, Ma’s next goal is to make the robot sturdier, smaller, and more versatile. Once it’s portable enough, it can be used outside dedicated waste facilities, opening up a whole other world of use cases.

“Once it’s smaller, it can be used as a stand-alone recycling solution for events, for shopping centers, hospitals, or airports to recycle their waste at the source,” Ma told TechCrunch, “and that’s the way we can really change how we’re managing our packaging waste.”

articles.summary: Watch as Equity discusses whether ditching NDAs will change how data center deals get done, why trust may be the real product for personal AI startups, plus a couple of deals of the week.
articles.body:
Amazon says it will stop using NDAs when negotiating data center deals with local governments, following a similar move from Microsoft earlier this year. Secrecy has fueled community backlash against AI infrastructure, with opposition leading to hundreds of proposed and enacted moratoriums from New York to San Francisco. Meanwhile, a wave of startups is betting that consumers will hand AI agents access to their inboxes, files, and credit cards — if they can get websites to let them in .

On this episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast, Anthony Ha, Sean O’Kane, and Rebecca Bellan dig into whether ditching NDAs will change how data center deals get done, why trust may be the real product for personal AI startups, plus a couple of deals of the week.
